57 draft packages. Images have no embedded text; wording listed as an overlay is rendered separately.
ENC-D01-A · The lunch threat

At a diner, a trans driver reads May 2026’s counterterrorism strategy targeting violent groups described as “radically pro-transgender.” On TV, a pundit drops “violent.” The driver closes his lunch cooler. “There goes my weapons inspection.”
Use paper; save the actual wording → You use some paper to save the wording, head pounding. The driver opens lunch slowly. Apparently mayonnaise now needs witnesses.
Take the quick TV version → The simple version clears your head. By dessert, the pundit has promoted coleslaw to a sleeper cell.
Say all trans people were designated → He says no: the strategy does not designate all trans people. The pundit has already booked a second expert on sandwiches.

Scene: The driver closes a lunch cooler beside a public document while the travelers pause near the counter; a pundit gestures on a blank television. The ordinary lunch cooler occupies the foreground beneath the grandiose television performance.
Editable overlays: “MAY 2026 COUNTERTERRORISM STRATEGY” — Editable caption beside the blank public document
Source: Counterterrorism framing of trans advocacy — www.whitehouse.gov
ENC-D01-B · White, rye, or counsel

At a Pentagon-adjacent sandwich counter, a reporter shows March 2026’s revised press rules after a court struck parts down. The memo says asking questions isn’t criminal. The cashier asks white or rye. Three people check whether he’s credentialed.
Use paper; save the actual memo → You use paper to save the memo, head pounding. The cashier repeats the bread options slowly, as though negotiating access to a submarine.
Accept that the dispute is settled → You relax at the reassurance. The reporter corrects you: revised rules don’t settle every dispute. The sandwich still awaits clearance.
Say ingredient questions are forbidden → The reporter corrects you: the memo expressly says asking questions isn’t criminal. The cashier courageously reveals the existence of mustard.

Scene: The cashier holds two unbranded bread loaves apart while the reporter points to a blank public memo and travelers pause at the counter. An ordinary choice of bread receives the solemn scrutiny of a security briefing.
Editable overlays: “REVISED PRESS MEMO · MARCH 23, 2026” — Blank public memo
Source: Pentagon press-credential policy and judicial correction — media.defense.gov
ENC-D01-C · Your call is medically important

At a diner, an off-duty nurse asks your crew to document her hospital's response to CMS withdrawing emergency-abortion guidance: a legal hotline. She's testing it over breakfast. The waitress brings the phone its own menu. It's been here longer than anyone.
Use your paper; document the delay → You use some supplies to save the timed account, head aching. The waitress clears breakfast around the phone. It has qualified for lunch.
Accept the hotline's reassuring greeting → The recorded reassurance settles your head until the nurse explains it approves nothing. The waitress asks whether the recording wants its usual.
Say federal law requires this hotline → The nurse corrects you: the hospital invented the hotline. The waitress takes back its menu. House guests aren't federal officials.

Scene: The nurse shows the observing travelers a phone on speaker beside untouched toast while the waitress sets a blank menu upright beside it. A phone occupies a complete place setting with its own menu while a cold breakfast crowds the nurse's side of the table.
Editable overlays: “PLEASE HOLD” — Separate caption beside the phone, not part of its screen
Source: Emergency abortion exceptions and federal guidance withdrawal — cms.gov
Source: Emergency abortion exceptions and federal guidance withdrawal — capitol.texas.gov
Source: Emergency abortion exceptions and federal guidance withdrawal — capitol.texas.gov
ENC-D02-A · The house is still at large

Outside a courthouse, a volunteer asks your crew to help carry returned belongings. Her client was arrested after a miscarriage; the charges were dropped. Police kept the woman's house keys as evidence. Apparently her front door was an accessory.
Use some water; rest in shade → You drink some water and recover in the shade. The volunteer checks the returned keys. The house is still at large.
Help carry the returned-property box → You scrape your arms carrying the box. The volunteer checks its contents twice. An apology wasn't among the items police returned.
Share water; record the property delay → You share some water and record the arrest, dismissal and property delay. The volunteer turns the key. The door declines to resist release.

Scene: The volunteer indicates a sealed returned-property box on a trolley while holding a key ring; travelers consider helping beside an empty shaded bench. An oversized blank evidence tag still dangles from an ordinary house key after the case has ended.
Editable overlays: “RETURNED PROPERTY” — Blank tag on the sealed box
Source: Georgia miscarriage arrest followed by dismissal — themarshallproject.org
Source: Georgia miscarriage arrest followed by dismissal — walb.com
ENC-D02-B · The roof remains eligible

A school gym’s equipment sale draws you inside. The coach explains Trump’s sports order uses federal funding to exclude trans girls from girls’ teams. A leak drips onto the basketballs. Washington located the girl. Nobody located a roofer.
Use food and water; take a break → You use some food and water for a break, recovering. The coach moves a bucket. The roof remains eligible for every team.
Shift equipment away from the leak → You strain yourself shifting equipment out of the leak. The coach adds another bucket. It passes eligibility without a hearing.
Supply the coach’s public notice → You give paper and tape for a notice quoting the actual order. Above it, the leak continues its undefeated season.

Scene: The coach points to a public order beside unsold balls while a roof drip falls toward an existing bucket; travelers pause at the sale entrance. A row of ordinary buckets is doing more visible work than the oversized official-looking policy sheet.
Editable overlays: “PUBLIC EQUIPMENT SALE” — Blank entrance board; “FEDERAL SCHOOL-SPORTS ORDER” — Blank public notice
Source: Women's sports restrictions enforced through federal funding — www.whitehouse.gov
ENC-D02-C · An active workplace

At a nursing-home rummage sale, an aide points to federal staffing minimums repealed in February 2026. Older requirements remain. The administrator is selling extra chairs. His plan for keeping everybody on their feet is proceeding beautifully.
Use food and water; rest → You use food and water to rest and recover. The aide sits briefly. The chair demonstrates a suspiciously affordable retention strategy.
Help move the sale chairs → You strain yourself moving chairs. The administrator calls this proof fewer seats encourage activity. The aide offers him the heaviest one.
Supply an accurate public notice → You give paper and tape for an accurate notice. The aide adds the older requirements. The administrator’s uncluttered wall becomes less efficient.

Scene: The administrator presents several unsold chairs while the aide holds a public staffing notice and travelers consider the sale. The administrator alone has brought a luxurious folding seat behind the table.
Editable overlays: “PUBLIC RUMMAGE SALE” — Blank entrance board; “FEDERAL STAFFING REPEAL · FEBRUARY 2026” — Blank public notice
Source: New nursing-home staffing minimums repealed — regulations.justia.com
ENC-D03-A · Tell the airbags
At a rest stop, a trans Kansas driver shows the replacement license the state required. Same driver. Same car. Different sex marker. He asks whether he needs to notify the airbags.
Use paper; save the law’s scope → You use paper to save the law’s actual scope. He puts the new card away. The camera still remembers who it photographed.
Share lunch with the driver → You share lunch and laugh. His car unlocks without consulting his birth certificate. Even the door recognizes him.
Take a quiet bench break → You clear your head on a quiet bench. He adjusts the driver’s seat. It still has the same opinion of his legs.

Scene: The worker keeps all details of a blank replacement card covered while pointing toward a public law printout; travelers listen beside the picnic area. His face and the obscured card occupy parallel positions, with an ordinary car door waiting behind him.
Editable overlays: “KANSAS · REPLACEMENT LICENSE” — Editable caption beside blank public law
Source: Kansas links bathroom enforcement to invalidated identity documents — www.kslegislature.gov
Source: Kansas links bathroom enforcement to invalidated identity documents — www.ksrevenue.gov
ENC-D03-B · The toaster has a floor

At a thrift store, a visiting disabled worker shows July 2025’s abandoned federal phaseout of subminimum-wage certificates. His employer uses one where state law permits. Here, the donated toaster enjoys a firm minimum price.
Use paper; save the federal rule → You use paper to save the federal rule. He turns the toaster over. Even secondhand appliances receive a proper valuation.
Share a full lunch → You share lunch and laugh. He checks the toaster’s warranty. Lasting thirty days apparently earns more confidence than working every weekday.
Take a quiet break → You take a quiet break. The cashier refuses a lower offer for the toaster. Some labor-saving devices must never be undervalued.

Scene: The worker examines an unplugged donated toaster’s blank price card while offering a public federal notice; travelers browse beside him. The cashier protects the toaster’s price card with the firmness missing from the worker’s wage policy.
Editable overlays: “PRICE FIRM” — Blank toaster price tag; “FEDERAL PHASEOUT WITHDRAWN · JULY 2025” — Blank public notice
Source: Federal phaseout of disabled-worker subminimum-wage certificates abandoned — regulations.justia.com
Source: Federal phaseout of disabled-worker subminimum-wage certificates abandoned — www.dol.gov
ENC-D03-C · Roadworthy, pending counsel

At a motel breakfast, adult volunteers review Idaho's restrictions on concealed abortion assistance to unemancipated minors. They ask your crew to record the public facts for D.C. Their car passed its inspection. The route needs a lawyer. The lawyer doesn't do roadside assistance.
Use your paper; record the limits → You use some supplies to save the minor-specific limits. The driver files the car's clean inspection beside the questions keeping it parked.
Share food with the planning volunteers → You share some food and enjoy lunch together. The lawyer unrolls the route papers. The driver puts the bread basket on them. Lunch proceeds.
Read quietly on the motel porch → You clear your head on the porch. The car wears a cheerful roadworthy sticker. Its driver is still inside, qualifying the journey.

Scene: A volunteer shows an inspection sheet and broad, unmarked route map to the observing travelers; the lawyer waits beside an untouched bread basket. A small vehicle inspection sheet lies beside a much larger set of legal questions while the inspected car remains visibly parked outside.
Editable overlays: “VEHICLE INSPECTION: PASSED” — Blank inspection-sheet heading; “IDAHO MINOR-ASSISTANCE LAW” — Blank legal folder heading
Source: Idaho restrictions on abortion assistance to minors — cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov
Source: Idaho restrictions on abortion assistance to minors — litigationtracker.law.georgetown.edu
ENC-D04-A · Small government, large pants

At an outdoor shop, a trans hunting-club treasurer shows you ATF’s proposed birth-sex rule for its forms. The owner wants Washington out of his gun cabinet. He is considerably more flexible about somebody else’s pants.
Read the actual proposal → You check the proposal’s limits. The owner hides his sales ledger when you glance at it. Certain personal details are sacred.
Save the public notice → You save the notice, head aching. The owner locks his office. His small-government tour has reached its border.
Trust the total-ban rumor → The treasurer corrects you: this proposal does not ban all trans gun owners. The owner still pats his cabinet protectively.

Scene: The treasurer offers the public notice to the observing travelers while the owner closes a blank ledger beside his locked office. The owner guards his own paperwork with both arms while leaning toward somebody else’s public forms.
Editable overlays: “ATF PROPOSED RULE · MAY 2026” — Editable caption above the blank public notice
Source: Gun-rights promises and ATF identity paperwork — www.atf.gov
ENC-D04-B · Housing, with a lock

At a camping shop, an outreach worker reads Trump’s July 2025 order promoting broader civil commitment through legal and funding changes. It isn’t automatic confinement. The display tent has three bedrooms. Her clients keep getting offered plans with locks.
Read what the order actually directs → You check the order’s limits. The worker measures the display tent. It remains the most detailed housing proposal in the room.
Save the public order → You save the order, head aching. The salesman demonstrates a zipper from the inside. Choosing when to leave appears to be a feature.
Call it automatic confinement for everyone → The worker corrects you: legal processes and criteria still matter. The government’s sweeping announcement came with much smaller print.

Scene: The outreach worker compares a public order with the display tent while the salesperson holds its entrance open and travelers browse nearby. The inviting tent doorway is much larger than the small official-looking policy sheet beside it.
Editable overlays: “DISPLAY TENT” — Blank retail card; “FEDERAL ORDER · JULY 2025” — Blank public policy sheet
Source: Homelessness order promotes expanded civil commitment — www.whitehouse.gov
ENC-D04-C · The purpose of a sandwich

A Texas volunteer at a roadside café asks your crew to check SB33: public abortion-travel assistance includes food. The café owner is preparing a city-convention catering bid. He holds up one sandwich. Apparently he needs to know where it plans to go after lunch.
Check the public-spending limits → You verify the limits. The owner puts the sandwich beside his catering forms. It qualifies for public money by staying vague about its itinerary.
Save the food-assistance provision → You save the provision, head aching. The owner cuts the sandwich diagonally. It has changed direction without resolving its funding status.
Post that private food donations are banned → The volunteer corrects you: SB33 targets public assistance. The owner removes your claim from the table before it frightens the bread.

Scene: The owner holds a whole sandwich over a blank catering form while the volunteer offers a public source to the observing travelers. An ordinary sandwich sits where a formal applicant's headshot would go on an oversized blank catering application.
Editable overlays: “PUBLIC CATERING BID” — Blank folder header
Source: Texas restrictions on public abortion-travel assistance — capitol.texas.gov
Source: Texas restrictions on public abortion-travel assistance — texasattorneygeneral.gov
ENC-D05-A · A lifetime warranty

A visiting Louisiana nurse asks your crew to time a cabinet lock at a hardware store. State controls now secure misoprostol, also used to stop bleeding. The salesman offers a lifetime warranty. She would settle for getting it open before closing.
Check the rule and reported delays → You verify the rule and reported delays, head aching. The salesman offers another key. The nurse asks whether it comes with another afternoon.
Browse the quiet garden aisle → You clear your head by the garden supplies. The salesman demonstrates a watering can. Its contents escape without finding a supervisor.
Say the medicine is completely banned → The simple story settles your head until she corrects it: valid prescribing remains lawful. The salesman resumes wrestling with the lawful cabinet.

Scene: The salesman tries a key in an empty demonstration cabinet while the nurse holds a timing device and travelers watch without assisting. A giant warranty ribbon hangs from a small cabinet whose demonstration door will not open.
Editable overlays: “LIFETIME WARRANTY” — Blank sales ribbon
Source: Louisiana controls on mifepristone and misoprostol — legis.la.gov
Source: Louisiana controls on mifepristone and misoprostol — nola.gov
Source: Louisiana controls on mifepristone and misoprostol — lawyeringproject.org
ENC-D05-B · The phone plan stays

At a pharmacy café, a parent reads the Medicaid and CHIP youth transition-care exclusions due October 13, 2026. Some existing hormone care gets up to six extra months. Her teenager keeps growing. The phone plan renews automatically.
Read the dates and funding limits → You check the dates and exceptions, head aching. The phone company has committed to her longer than the benefits department.
Take a quiet window seat → You clear your head by the window. Her phone renews with a cheerful ping. Apparently continuity is available as an add-on.
Use the headline; take a break → The short version feels manageable until she corrects it: funding exclusions, not a ban on all care. Your certainty expires first.

Scene: The parent compares a blank policy sheet with her blank phone screen while the travelers wait at the café counter. A tiny phone renewal notification sits beside the much larger federal exclusion document, as though the phone offers the longer commitment.
Editable overlays: “FEDERAL FUNDING RULE · EFFECTIVE OCTOBER 13, 2026” — Blank public policy sheet; “PLAN RENEWED” — Blank phone screen; no account or personal details
Source: Upcoming Medicaid and CHIP treatment-payment exclusion — www.govinfo.gov
ENC-D05-C · Still part of the family

A retired municipal worker at a diner shows June 2025’s Supreme Court ruling limiting disabled retirees’ employment-discrimination claims. Other protections remain. His old workplace still calls him family. Benefits would like to know whether he’s currently employed by this family.
Read the actual employment limits → You read the job-holding limits, head aching. His retirement photograph has room for everybody except the person calculating the benefits.
Take a quiet break → You take a quiet break. He folds the workplace-family brochure into a coaster. It finally supports something.
Trust the warm brochure → You trust the warm brochure and relax. He corrects your legal summary. The family reunion has an eligibility date.

Scene: The retiree holds a generic workplace-family brochure beside the public court ruling while travelers wait near the counter. An exuberant group-photo silhouette on the blank brochure contrasts with a tiny isolated chair at the end of the table.
Editable overlays: “ALWAYS PART OF THE FAMILY” — Blank retirement brochure; “SUPREME COURT · JUNE 2025” — Blank public ruling
Source: Disabled retirees' employment-discrimination claim meets the job-holding requirement — www.supremecourt.gov
ENC-D06-A · The federal wardrobe case
At a post office, a woman explains how June 2026’s court order restored her trans sister’s care and clothing in federal prison. She needs a stamp. Her sister needed a federal judge to get dressed.
Read and save the public ruling → You save the ruling, head aching. Her sister’s care needed a judge. The postage merely wants money.
Give paper for the public order → You give paper for the public order; her sister’s details stay private. The wardrobe dispute has grown another stack of stationery.
Take a quiet break outside → You clear your head outside. She seals the envelope. Ordinary glue remains one of the few accommodations requiring no litigation.

Scene: The woman holds the public ruling beside a blank copier tray; her sealed private envelope remains face down, and travelers observe from the public counter. A small sealed envelope is dwarfed by the public legal papers resting beside it; its address is hidden.
Editable overlays: “PUBLIC COURT RULING · JUNE 17, 2026” — Blank public document cover
Source: Federal prison care and personal-item restrictions — law.justia.com
Source: Federal prison care and personal-item restrictions — www.markey.senate.gov
ENC-D06-B · A cleaner angle

At a hardware counter, a power-plant neighbor reads EPA’s February 2026 repeal of stronger mercury and toxic-metal rules. Older limits survive. The salesman makes a dirty demonstration filter look cleaner by turning it around. Government innovation travels fast.
Read and save the remaining limits → You save the remaining limits and repealed requirements, head aching. The salesman turns the filter back. The dirt declines to renegotiate.
Use paper for an accurate notice → You use paper for an accurate notice. The neighbor draws the filter’s dirty side. The salesman calls it an unfair angle.
Take a quiet break outside → You clear your head outside. Through the window, the same filter is enjoying a second immaculate face.

Scene: The salesperson rotates a two-sided demonstration filter while the neighbor holds the public EPA notice and travelers browse. The filter’s clean face points toward the sales counter while its visibly dirty side faces away.
Editable overlays: “EPA RULE · FEBRUARY 2026” — Blank public notice
Source: Stronger coal-plant mercury and toxic-metal standards repealed — www.federalregister.gov
ENC-D06-C · The complimentary lullaby

At a rest stop, an Alabama couple asks your crew to check the embryo ruling and later IVF-clinic immunity law. Their own insurance excludes IVF. The agent on speaker calls children priceless. He has priced everything required to have one.
Check and save the legal distinction → You save the ruling and immunity limits, head aching. The agent congratulates them on the embryos' status. They ask where to redeem it.
Use your paper; copy the limits → You use some supplies to copy the limits. They fold the agent's smiling-baby brochure over the exclusions. The baby is sitting on the bill.
Leave the call for some quiet → You clear your head away from the call. The hold music plays a lullaby. The couple has been receiving it for free.

Scene: The couple indicates a blank insurance booklet beside a phone on speaker while travelers consider checking the public legal sources. An idyllic generic baby image on an insurance brochure covers a visibly dense block of blank exclusion lines.
Editable overlays: “IVF EXCLUDED” — Editable label on the blank policy-summary area
Source: Alabama frozen-embryo wrongful-death ruling and IVF immunity — law.justia.com
Source: Alabama frozen-embryo wrongful-death ruling and IVF immunity — apnews.com
ENC-D07-A · Rewards for coming back empty

A traveler at a rest stop asks your crew to check Arizona's emergency-contraception refusal rule. The pharmacy returned her prescription, as required. It also offered a loyalty card. She holds them side by side. They are building a lasting relationship with the paper.
Check and save the actual rule → You save the refusal-and-return rule, clearing the confusion. She folds the loyalty card around the prescription. It finally supports contraception.
Say Arizona banned emergency contraception → She corrects you: the law permits specified refusals. She hasn't come this far to collect another person saying no.
Use your paper; copy the limits → You use some supplies to copy the limits. She tucks them into the loyalty-card sleeve. The free gift finally contains useful information.

Scene: The traveler holds an unmarked prescription sheet and a blank loyalty card side by side while current crew members listen. The polished promotional sleeve is much larger than the small piece of care information returned with it.
Editable overlays: “LOYALTY REWARDS” — Blank promotional card heading
Source: Arizona conscience refusal for emergency contraception
ENC-D07-B · The invisible emergency

At a copy shop, a trans mechanic reads Social Security’s June 2026 rule: its sex field can only be changed to reflect sex at birth. It isn’t printed on the card. Washington has discovered his most urgent component: invisible paperwork.
Save the actual records rule → You save the rule and clear up the confusion. He holds the card to the light. Still no sex field. Tremendous progress.
Assume the card displays it → He corrects you and covers the personal details. The blank space remains flawless. The federal government has defended it at considerable length.
Use paper for the public rule → You use your paper for the public rule. He puts it beside the card. The invisible field now requires visible luggage.

Scene: The mechanic compares a covered blank card with a long public policy sheet while travelers wait near the copier. A tiny card with no visible sex field lies beside a vastly larger pile of instructions about that field.
Editable overlays: “SSA RECORDS RULE · JUNE 2026” — Blank public instruction sheet
Source: Social Security's invisible sex field is frozen to birth records — secure.ssa.gov
ENC-D07-C · The website gets an extension

At a library printer, a low-vision resident reads DOJ’s April 2026 extension of government-web accessibility deadlines into 2027 and 2028. Existing access duties remain. Her appointment confirmation is due today. The website has successfully requested an accommodation.
Save the actual deadlines → You save the deadlines and clear up the confusion. Her appointment still needs confirming. Only the website has been excused from showing up.
Assume all access duties are suspended → She corrects you: existing access duties remain. The government gave its website more time, not permission to stop being a government.
Use paper for a large-type copy → You use paper for a large-type public notice. She checks the dates. Enlarging the words proves considerably faster than enlarging the deadline.

Scene: The resident holds a public notice near a reading aid while a blank computer screen and printer sit beside the observing travelers. A large, comfortable office chair belongs to the uncooperative public computer; the resident stands beside a small stool.
Editable overlays: “PUBLIC WEB DEADLINES · 2027 / 2028” — Blank public notice
Source: Government website accessibility deadlines extended — www.ada.gov
Source: Government website accessibility deadlines extended — www.ada.gov
ENC-D08-A · Two functioning arms

At a pregnancy center's open house, a nurse asks your crew to check its ads against Massachusetts's warnings about misleading centers. The manager offers a 'medical volunteer' badge for carrying a sandwich board. The qualifications are two functioning arms. The center offers no abortion referrals.
Use your paper; check the services → You use some supplies to check the missing services, head pounding. The manager offers a lab coat. Apparently it covers the gaps.
Carry the sign; endorse the center → You scrape your shin and relax into the pitch. The nurse corrects your endorsement: no abortion referrals. Your badge doesn't cover that either.
Leave without checking the claims → You leave with a quieter head and no checked account. The manager hangs your unused badge on the sandwich board. Staffing restored.

Scene: The manager offers an unworn blank badge toward the observing travelers beside a leaning sandwich board while the nurse holds a public agency fact sheet. The large badge and spare white coat are ready before any qualifications have been discussed; the board's metal feet protrude visibly.
Editable overlays: “MEDICAL VOLUNTEER” — Blank offered badge; “OPEN HOUSE” — Blank sandwich-board header
Source: Pregnancy-center advertising and service mismatch — mass.gov
Source: Pregnancy-center advertising and service mismatch — mass.gov
ENC-D08-B · Family first, calendar later

At a union-hall table sale, a worker shows May 2025’s ruling removing certain abortion accommodations from the federal pregnancy-workplace rule. Medical-treatment exceptions remain. A manager selling “FAMILY FIRST” mugs promises unlimited time off, provided time stops first.
Use paper; check the actual limits → You save the actual limits using paper, drained. The manager removes the clock batteries. His generous leave policy is nearly operational.
Trust him; help stack tables → The simple promise clears your head. You strain yourself stacking tables, then learn the manager’s unlimited leave exists only on mugs.
Skip the details; take a break → You relax, then repeat that every pregnancy protection vanished. The worker corrects you. The mug is still the least complicated witness.

Scene: The manager presents a blank mug beside folded tables while the worker offers the public ruling and travelers browse. A large cheerful mug sits beneath an ordinary wall clock with a blank face and simple hands; the battery cover is visible but untouched.
Editable overlays: “FAMILY FIRST” — Blank mug; editable lettering only; “PUBLIC RULING · MAY 2025” — Blank court document
Source: Workplace abortion accommodations removed from the PWFA regulation — cases.justia.com
Source: Workplace abortion accommodations removed from the PWFA regulation — apnews.com
ENC-D08-C · Same water, happier label

At a water-filter shop, a utility worker reads EPA’s May 2026 proposals to drop some PFAS limits and extend certain deadlines. Nothing is final. The salesman presents two identical demonstration samples. One has a much more optimistic label.
Use paper; check the actual proposals → You use paper to save the proposals, drained. The salesman swaps the labels. The samples achieve an immediate regulatory breakthrough.
Trust him; help carry display boxes → His assurance clears your head. You strain yourself carrying boxes before the worker corrects his claims. The optimism weighs more than advertised.
Take the headline; take a break → You relax, then describe the proposals as final. The worker corrects you. The salesman has already printed the victory stickers.

Scene: The salesperson holds blank tags beside two sealed clear-water display bottles while the worker points to a public proposal and travelers consider the counter. Identical display samples are treated as opposites because one blank tag has a cheerful decorative border.
Editable overlays: “OPTIMISTIC” — Blank decorative display tag; “EPA PROPOSALS · MAY 2026” — Blank public notice
Source: EPA proposes removing some PFAS drinking-water limits and delaying others — www.epa.gov
Source: EPA proposes removing some PFAS drinking-water limits and delaying others — www.epa.gov
ENC-D09-A · Reserved for the return trip

Your crew stops at a hospital's public meeting about losing maternity services. A volunteer shows the national maternity-care desert report. The county commissioner unveils reserved parking for new mothers. From those spaces, it's a long drive to somewhere they can become one.
Check the closure and remaining services → You check the closure and remaining services, head aching. The commissioner measures the parking bay. The route to a delivery ward won't fit.
Take a quiet look at the garden → You clear your head in the garden. The commissioner tests the parking ribbon again. It is the only local delivery he has scheduled.
Rest in the van instead → You nap and miss the community account. The commissioner posts his parking photograph, cropped just above the shuttered maternity windows.

Scene: The commissioner holds a ribbon across an empty reserved bay while the volunteer offers a broad service map to the observing travelers. A carefully decorated new-mother parking space faces a closed former maternity entrance.
Editable overlays: “NEW MOTHERS” — Blank reserved-parking sign; “MATERNITY SERVICES RELOCATED” — Blank former-entrance notice
Source: Maternity-care deserts and loss of local birth services — marchofdimes.org
Source: Maternity-care deserts and loss of local birth services — www2.marchofdimes.org
ENC-D09-B · The cheaper repair

At a phone-repair counter, a youth volunteer revises referral cards: the specialized LGBTQ+ option within 988 closed July 17, 2025; the general line remains. Washington called it ending separate services. The clerk calls removing buttons a cheaper repair.
Check the agency and operator notices → You check both notices, head aching. The clerk points at a phone missing a button. It also serves everyone equally now.
Take a quiet break outside → You clear your head outside. The clerk is still waiting to hear how fewer specialists became a larger welcome.
Skim the headline; nap → You nap, then repeat that 988 closed. The volunteer corrects you. Your shortcut has disconnected the service that remains.

Scene: The volunteer keeps blank referral cards and public notices on the counter while the clerk indicates an unpowered demonstration phone missing a button; travelers observe. The visibly incomplete demonstration phone sits on a neat repair cushion like an officially improved product.
Editable overlays: “GENERAL 988 SERVICE CONTINUES” — Blank public referral card; “SPECIALIZED LGBTQ+ YOUTH OPTION CLOSED JULY 17, 2025” — Blank public notice
Source: Closure of specialized LGBTQ+ youth crisis-line service — www.samhsa.gov
Source: Closure of specialized LGBTQ+ youth crisis-line service — 988lifeline.org
ENC-D09-C · A longer planning horizon

At a rest-area picnic table, a Women’s Health Initiative participant shows April 2025’s funding cancellation and May’s reversal. The study continued. She’s kept appointments for decades. Her bagged salad has a longer planning horizon than Washington.
Read the cancellation and reversal → You check the timeline, head aching. She puts the cancellation under her salad container. It has finally helped preserve something.
Take a quiet bench break → You clear your head on a quiet bench. She checks next year’s appointment. The salad is the only thing legitimately expiring.
Skim the cancellation; nap → You nap and repeat that the study closed. She corrects you. Your obituary arrived before her next appointment reminder.

Scene: The participant lays public cancellation and reversal notices beside an unopened salad container while travelers pause at the table. The orderly lunch container sits between two official-looking notices that visibly point in opposite directions through their paper folds.
Editable overlays: “APRIL 2025: NONRENEWAL” — First blank public notice; “MAY 2025: REVERSED; STUDY CONTINUES” — Second blank public notice
Source: Women's Health Initiative funding cancellation reversed — www.whi.org
ENC-D10-A · Freedom at whisper volume

While you price copies, a trans warehouse worker reads EEOC’s January 2026 decision rescinding harassment guidance. Discrimination law survives. A supervisor asks whether he can say anything now. The clerk switches on the security microphone.
Use paper; save the agency statement → You use paper to save the agency’s statement. The supervisor lowers his voice. Remarkable how quickly clarification improves working conditions.
Wait quietly by the door → You wait by the door and clear your head. The supervisor tests a whisper. His new freedom requires very little volume.
Accept the supervisor’s interpretation → The worker corrects you: the law remains. The supervisor asks if the camera records sound. His confidence needs terms and conditions.

Scene: The clerk’s hand rests on a microphone switch as the supervisor leans toward the counter and the worker holds the public notice; travelers compare blank copy-price cards. The supervisor’s expansive posture contracts under a tiny microphone.
Editable overlays: “EEOC NOTICE · JANUARY 2026” — Blank public notice
Source: EEOC rescinds workplace harassment guidance — www.eeoc.gov
ENC-D10-B · The crayon checkpoint

Take a quiet break → You clear your head outside. The volunteer returns to sorting crayons. Her original job has survived another attempt to make it something else.
Trust the headline about new checks → The volunteer corrects you: the injunction blocks the Head Start restriction. The crayons have already returned to their previous profession.

Trust the brochure’s safety promise → You endorse the brochure. She turns it over: a warranty for the camera, nothing for the person underneath.

At a highway pharmacy, a clerk offers detour directions while recalling Biden’s January 2025 withdrawal of proposed prescription-free contraceptive coverage. Existing rules remained. The medicine was already on the shelf. The insurance card wanted it to visit a doctor.
Follow the clerk’s direct detour → The direct detour regains time and clears your head. The clerk’s map has a startling innovation: only one place marked destination.

Check the ruling; take side streets → You confirm the ruling’s limits and recover some time on side streets. The volunteer appreciates a route that discloses its destination.

ENC-D12-B · Destination included

At a bus-station café, a travel-aid volunteer offers directions while reading March 2026’s stay of a third-country deportation ruling. A chance to contest the destination remains disputed. At the ticket desk, that privilege comes with the cheap seats.
Use paper for the quick road route → You copy the quick road route using some paper and regain time. The volunteer circles the destination. Your itinerary has advanced civil rights.
Check the status; take the slower shortcut → You verify the ruling’s status and take the slower shortcut. The volunteer confirms where you’re going. No one calls this radical.

Share food; take his direct directions → You share food and take his direct road directions. He can repair the screen; the audience assembled behind it is another department.
Check the settlement before leaving → You regain some road and credibility. The technician can replace a cracked screen faster than an advertiser can forget a useful secret.

The FTC banned X-Mode’s sale of sensitive location data. At a roadside café, a promoter insists location dots are anonymous. The waitress points to the clinic across the street. He offers to make the dots smaller.

ENC-D13-B · The tolerant detour sign

At a Beltway road closure, a reporter recalls 2025’s White House restrictions on AP over “Gulf of Mexico.” Access was still disputed that November. The detour sign is more tolerant: it lets you disagree with the arrows.
Follow the reporter’s main-road detour → The reporter’s directions recover time. The road accepts your destination without testing whether you’ve used the president’s preferred name for the water.
Take the quiet side streets → You regain some time and clear your head. The reporter waves goodbye. No test of your publication’s ocean vocabulary.

Take his quieter side streets → You regain some time and clear your head. He caps a clean pipe fitting. Still waiting on the government’s matching part.

ENC-W-MW-D01-A · The chairs retain their value

A surplus dealer offers $14 to sort office chairs. A researcher says NIH cancelled her gender-identity research grant in 2025. Washington found the work worthless. The dealer finds a lever beneath her chair and immediately sees its potential.
Sort chairs; keep the public ruling → You earn $14 and save the ruling, drained. The dealer finds the chairs extremely useful now nobody is thinking in them.
Share food and exchange contacts → You share food and swap contacts. She corrects your account of the funding fight. The dealer prices her chair above her expertise.
Take a quiet break → You take a quiet break. A customer sits in the best chair and announces that science has gone too far.

Sort the receipt rolls for $14 → You earn $14 and save the rule, head aching. Their combined safety cushion has lost a corner to the wedding.
Share food; compare the exemptions → You share food, gain a contact, and check exemptions. They agree the cake was easier to divide than legal permission to save.
Take a quiet break outside → Your head clears outside. The shop sells two-for-one wedding cards, which is still less aggressive arithmetic than the benefits rule.

ENC-W-MW-D01-C · Both hands of government

A community print shop offers $14 to sort benefit leaflets. A volunteer points to September 18, 2026’s upcoming public-charge rule, broadening certain immigration reviews. Exceptions remain. One government leaflet offers help; another asks why anybody would need it.
Sort leaflets; keep the public rule → You earn $14 and keep the public rule, drained. Both leaflets feature welcoming hands. They point in opposite directions.
Share paper and exchange contacts → You share paper and swap contacts with the volunteer. She marks the actual exceptions. The helping hand requires an instruction manual.
Take a quiet break → You take a quiet break. The volunteer puts both leaflets on one stand. One open hand has developed a pointing finger.

Scene: The printer indicates two unsorted leaflet stacks with blank covers and generic hand illustrations while the volunteer holds the public rule and travelers consider the offer. Two cheerful illustrated helping hands point away from each other across the same counter.

ENC-W-MW-D02-A · Storage is thriving

A freight depot offers $12 to shift empty coolers. A dispatcher reads June 2026’s USAID audit: cancelled distribution left contraceptives deteriorating in Belgium while storage bills grew. The empty coolers are still receiving excellent logistical support.
Read and save the public audit → You save the audit, drained. The warehouse charges by the day. Uncertainty has proved far more durable than the stock.
Shift the empty coolers → You earn $12 and strain your back shifting coolers. The empty ones are marked urgent. That seems to have helped.
Leave the freight job → You leave discouraged. The dispatcher checks another storage invoice. At least someone has found a reliable form of aid.

ENC-W-MW-D02-B · Some assembly required

A warehouse offers $12 to move bed frames. A tenant volunteer explains HUD’s February 2026 proposal to limit mixed-status families’ prorated housing aid; it isn’t final. The beds come in halves for assembly. Families are proving less cooperative.

Move the bed frames → You earn $12 moving bed frames and strain your back. Every frame expects the whole sleeper to arrive.
Leave the moving job → You leave discouraged. The volunteer puts the proposal beside the assembly instructions. Only one admits you’ll need help.

ENC-W-MW-D02-C · The car is a survivor

At a used-car lot, a buyer shares a redacted credit refusal after the federal medical-debt rule was scrapped. The dealer offers $12 to move wheels. The car’s three previous accidents require less explanation than the hospital bill.
Compare the ruling with public terms → You save the public terms, head aching. Three crashes are character; one hospital bill apparently makes a person unreliable.
Move the wheels for $12 → You earn $12 and a sore back. The dealer calls the damaged car a survivor, then refuses the human version financing.
Leave the car lot → You leave angry. The dealer puts another certified sticker on the car and asks the customer for more proof.

Scene: Dealer gestures toward unmoved spare wheels while buyer holds a redacted letter beside a visibly repaired display car. The patched car wears a grand certification ribbon while the living applicant faces more questions.

Source: Federal medical-debt reporting rule vacated
ENC-W-PC-D01-A · The camera recognizes you

Trump’s passport rules can force a trans applicant’s documents to disagree. At a photo shop, a clerk offers $16 to fold public guidance sheets. The camera recognizes the customer; the government needs older evidence.
Fold the guides for $16 → You earn $16 and save the public rule, head aching. The photo must resemble the applicant; the sex marker apparently needn’t.
Share food with the customer → You share food, laugh, and exchange numbers. The customer suggests a baby photo so both fields can be equally current.
Leave the folding job → You leave the job. The clerk checks the lighting again. It remains easier to correct a shadow than a federal document.

Scene: Clerk offers unfolded public guides while customer stands beside the idle camera; all personal documents remain closed. The camera sees the present customer while the public form requests evidence from the past.
Editable overlays: “$16 GUIDE FOLDING” — work card; “PASSPORT SEX-MARKER POLICY” — public guide heading; “CURRENT PHOTO” — camera-area placard
Source: Passport sex-marker restrictions
ENC-W-PC-D01-B · The boots can stay

A workwear shop offers $16 to sort boots. A trans Navy technician shows April 2026 separation guidance: covered personnel cannot use SkillBridge job training, with retention waivers possible. Behind him, a recruiting poster begs for his exact skills.
Sort the boots; keep the guidance → You earn $16 and save the guidance, drained. The boots have a simpler route back to useful service.
Share food and contact details → You share food and swap numbers. He offers job leads. The recruitment poster has contributed neither lunch nor a phone number.
Leave the sorting job → You leave the boots for someone else. The poster keeps recruiting the man standing underneath it.

Source: Military discharge and loss of transition-to-work assistance — law.justia.com
ENC-W-PC-D01-C · A legally supported welcome

Stack chairs; save the public ruling → You earn $16 and save the ruling, drained. Every chair folds the same way. The protection surrounding it doesn’t.
Share food and exchange numbers → You share food and exchange numbers. The organizer introduces you by first name. Lunch survives without a jurisdictional chart.
Leave the chair job → You leave the chairs to someone else. The welcome mat remains impressively fluent in promises.

ENC-W-PC-D02-A · Privacy begins at voting age

At a print counter, a visiting California teacher explains March 2026’s limited ruling on trans student identity disclosures. A campaigner offers $8 to hang flyers demanding every trans student’s identity. His phone lights up. He turns it face down.

Hang the campaigner’s flyers → You earn $8 spreading his blanket claim. The teacher corrects it. He asks you not to print his personal number.
Take a quiet break outside → You clear your head outside. Inside, the man selling total disclosure has moved his phone under the table.

ENC-W-PC-D02-B · Thank you, minus the treatment page

VA limits starting gender-affirming hormones while preserving specified exceptions. At an army-surplus shop, a veteran discusses the cutoff. The owner offers $8 to remove the restrictions page from benefit folders. The thank-you-for-your-service page stays.
Compare and save the public pages → You keep the public pages, mentally drained. Gratitude gets glossy paper; the missing treatment rule gets the shredder.
Remove the restrictions pages for $8 → You earn $8 and lose trust. The folders now thank veterans in color and disappoint them by appointment.
Step outside for a break → Your head clears outside. The owner calls the thinner folder less confusing, which is true until anyone tries to use it.

ENC-W-PC-D02-C · An independent mute button

A bar offers $8 to hang “NO CENSORSHIP” flyers. Its comic recalls Kimmel’s brief September 2025 suspension after FCC pressure; Carr disputed responsibility. The owner tests the microphone. It works beautifully until somebody says the chairman’s name.

Hang the owner’s flyers → You earn $8 backing the owner’s blanket claim. He mutes the sound check. The flyers remain impressively outspoken.
Take a quiet break outside → You clear your head outside. Through the window, the owner tests mute again. Freedom keeps passing the silent portion.

ENC-W-SW-D01-A · A better angle on homelessness

At a camping-supply yard, a resident challenges a local ticket after 2024’s Grants Pass ruling allowed general camping penalties. A contractor offers $10 to arrange barriers for a victory photo. His camera is aimed away from the tents.
Read the ruling’s actual limits → You read the ruling’s limits, head aching. The resident files the ticket carefully. It is the most expensive piece of shelter available.
Share food and water; rest → You share food and water, rest, and swap numbers. The resident saves you a seat. It requires no enforcement budget.
Haul barriers for the victory photo → You earn $10 hauling barriers, strain your back, and help sell the photo. The contractor thanks you for moving the problem eight feet.

ENC-W-SW-D01-B · The treaty fitting

ENC-D01-A · The lunch threat
At a diner, a trans driver reads May 2026’s counterterrorism strategy targeting violent groups described as “radically pro-transgender.” On TV, a pundit drops “violent.” The driver closes his lunch cooler. “There goes my weapons inspection.”
Use paper; save the actual wording → You use some paper to save the wording, head pounding. The driver opens lunch slowly. Apparently mayonnaise now needs witnesses.
